drafts.title: $0 and my hands stay on the wheel. Gemini can read your email in the car now. Grok rides in my Model Y. (pack AP2, AI for normal people)
drafts.window: Today ~12-1 PM ET (10-11 AM MT) at a charging stop, inside the warm band. Backup Thu ~8 PM.
drafts.angle: Pixel guy on a 1,500 mile drive, and Google just shipped "ask your car about your own stuff." Calm and practical: what it does, that it's opt-in, which one he'd actually use behind the wheel. Not a privacy scare (his ChatGPT profiling quote is already live).
bullets: Google, Oct 20, 2026: Gemini with Personal Intelligence rolling out on Android Auto starting that day; cars with Google built-in "in the coming months."
Google's examples: "What's my flight gate? Is my flight on time?" and "Take me to my doctor's appointment" (pulls the address from your calendar).
Opt-in and off by default; you pick which apps connect (Gmail, Calendar, Photos, Maps, YouTube, Search) and can turn it off in Gemini settings. Personal accounts 18+, not Workspace business accounts.
Grok in Tesla lost its beta label in 2026.38.5.10 (Not a Tesla App).
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
$0 and my hands stay on the wheel.

Google just let Gemini on Android Auto read your Gmail and calendar. Say "take me to my doctor's appointment" and it finds the address.

It's opt-in. You pick what it can see.

I've got Grok in my Model Y and a Pixel in my pocket. Today I asked Grok [___].

Would you let AI read your email in the car?

LONGER VERSION:
$0, and it's one less reason to pick up your phone while driving.

Google started rolling out Gemini with "Personal Intelligence" on Android Auto this week. It can look in your Gmail and calendar, so "is my flight on time?" or "take me to my doctor's appointment" just works. You don't have to dig for the confirmation email at a red light.

It's off until you turn it on, and you choose which apps it can see. You can shut it off any time.

For older drivers I think this is the real win. Fewer taps, fewer glances down.

I'm 1,500 miles into a road trip with Grok in my Model Y and a Pixel in my pocket. On this drive I've used Grok for [___]. I'd use Gemini for [___].

Would you let AI read your email in the car, or is that a line for you?

drafts.window: Thu ~8 PM (bright cell, he'll be on Central). Today's warm band works if F2/F3 slots are taken by driving.
drafts.angle: His own reply this week. He caught a cloned voice only because the room tone shifted, after 20+ years running sound. Most grandparents don't have that ear. The fix is free. Note: only name a family member if true. Replaces Tue's FBI 60+ $7.7B item; don't run both.
bullets: His reply: "The audio tone shifted when you stopped talking. It was either a cloned voice or you were in a sound proof studio." https://x.com/UpgradeAmerican/status/2112703584488005681
FTC: scammers need only a short clip of a family member's voice, often from social media, to clone it. Hang up and call back on a number you already have.
FCC: pick a family safe word ahead of time. AI-voice robocalls are illegal under the TCPA without consent.
FTC red flags: urgent, "keep it secret," pay by wire, crypto, gift cards, or payment app.
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:

I ran sound for over 20 years, and a cloned voice still almost fooled me this week. The only tell was the room tone.

[Most grandparents / my ___] wouldn't stand a chance.

[We set ours / We're picking ours this week.]

Does your family have one?

LONGER VERSION:
$0. That's the whole cost of the best scam protection your family can have.

This week I heard a voice clip that sounded exactly like the person. I only caught it because the background went dead silent when they stopped talking. I ran sound for bands and churches for over 20 years. That's the only reason I noticed.

Your grandkids' voices are all over social media. A scammer only needs a few seconds.

So here's our plan:
Hang up.
Call back on the number you already have.
Ask for the safe word.

[We set ours at ___ / We're picking ours this week.]

Does your family have a safe word yet?

drafts.title: $285 to $3,500. Solar you plug into a wall outlet, and a bill to let renters use it (pack AP6, renter solar, policy 1)
drafts.window: Mon ~3 PM once home (or an open warm-band slot this week). Not today; today belongs to the trip and earnings.
drafts.angle: The simplest solar there is. No roof, no installer. A new House bill would add rebates and protect renters. Bill-only, no party, sponsor stays in the link.
bullets: "Socket Full of Sunshine Act" introduced Oct 20, 2026 (House press release).
Typical plug-in system: 1 to 4 panels, $285 to $3,500 depending on size and battery; "hundreds of dollars a year" in savings (press release claim).

Would protect renters' right to use them, set safety standards, push states to drop utility approval fees, fund up to $1,000 state rebates for low and moderate income homes ($100M/yr DOE grants), and add a savings label.
10 states already have plug-in solar laws (Bright Saver, quoted in release). Only introduced, not law.

$285 to $3,500.

That's what solar you plug into a regular outlet costs. No roof. No installer. Renters too.

My rooftop system took a crew and a permit. [It cost me $___.]

10 states already allow plug-in solar. A new bill in Congress would push the rest.

Would you put panels on your balcony or fence if your landlord couldn't say no?

LONGER VERSION:
$285 to $3,500. That's the price range for solar that plugs into a regular wall outlet.

One to four panels on a balcony, a fence, or a patio. No roof work, no installer, and it goes with you when you move. That's a big deal if you rent, or if you're on a fixed income and can't swing a full system.

Ten states already allow it. A bill introduced this week would protect renters' right to use them, set safety rules, and fund rebates up to $1,000 for lower-income homes. It's only a bill so far.
